summary.text: For \(n\ge 21\), set \(d=D(n)\), \(r=D(d)\), and \(t=(n-r)/9\); congruence modulo \(9\) makes \(t\) integral, while complementary decimal blocks show that \(d(10^t-1)\) has digit sum \(9t\), so concatenating a copy of \(d\) produces a multiple \(k\) of \(D(n)\) with \(D(k)=n\). Thus \(k\) is a partner, or if \(k=n\), then \(10k\) is a distinct partner with the same digit sum; the cases \(1\le n<21\) are handled by an explicit finite list of partners.

full_proof.text:
Let \(D(m)\) denote the sum of the decimal digits of the nonnegative integer \(m\), with \(D(0)=0\). For a positive integer \(n\), call a positive integer \(k\) a partner of \(n\) if
\[
k\ne n,\qquad D(n)\mid k,\qquad D(k)\mid n.
\]
We prove that every positive \(n\) has such a partner. It will then follow immediately that the set from which \(a(n)\) is chosen is nonempty, so its least member is positive and hence \(a(n)\ne0\).

We first record the decimal digit facts used in the construction.

For every \(m\), writing \(m=10q+s\) with \(0\le s<10\), one has
\[
D(m)=s+D(q).
\]
Consequently, \(D(m)>0\) when \(m>0\), and \(D(m)\le m\). The latter inequality can also be seen inductively from the displayed recurrence. We will also use the sharper estimate
\[
D(m)\le \left\lfloor\frac m{10}\right\rfloor+9. \tag{1}
\]
Indeed, if \(q=\lfloor m/10\rfloor\) and \(s=m\bmod 10\), then
\[
D(m)=D(q)+s\le q+9.
\]
As usual, a number and its digit sum are congruent modulo \(9\):
\[
m\equiv D(m)\pmod 9. \tag{2}
\]
This follows by writing \(m\) as a sum of its digits times powers of \(10\), since \(10\equiv1\pmod9\).

We need three further elementary facts concerning decimal blocks.

First, if \(0\le x<10^t\), then for every \(y\ge0\),
\[
D(x+10^t y)=D(x)+D(y). \tag{3}
\]
The expression on the left is obtained by placing the decimal expansion of \(y\) to the left of a block of exactly \(t\) positions occupied by the digits of \(x\), with leading zeroes inserted into that block if necessary. Those inserted zeroes do not affect the digit sum, proving (3).

Second, for \(0\le x<10^t\),
\[
D(10^t-1-x)+D(x)=9t. \tag{4}
\]
This is the familiar complementary-digits identity, but we include an induction proof. For \(t=0\), the condition forces \(x=0\), and both sides are zero. For the induction step, write \(x=10q+s\), where \(0\le s\le9\) and \(q<10^t\). Then
\[
10^{t+1}-1-x
 =10(10^t-1-q)+(9-s).
\]
Thus its final digit is \(9-s\), while its remaining digits represent \(10^t-1-q\). Therefore
\[
\begin{aligned}
&D(10^{t+1}-1-x)+D(x)\\
&=D(10^t-1-q)+(9-s)+D(q)+s\\
&=9t+9=9(t+1),
\end{aligned}
\]
where the induction hypothesis was applied to \(q<10^t\).

Third, if \(d>0\) and \(d\le10^t\), then
\[
D\bigl(d(10^t-1)\bigr)=9t. \tag{5}
\]
To prove this, use the identity
\[
d(10^t-1)=(10^t-d)+10^t(d-1).
\]
Here \(0\le10^t-d<10^t\), so block additivity (3) gives
\[
D\bigl(d(10^t-1)\bigr)=D(10^t-d)+D(d-1).
\]
Because \(0\le d-1<10^t\), equation (4), applied to \(x=d-1\), says precisely that the last sum equals \(9t\).

We now construct a partner when \(n\ge21\). Set
\[
d=D(n),\qquad r=D(d),\qquad t=\frac{n-r}{9}.
\]
We must first justify that the last expression is a nonnegative integer and establish the bounds needed below. Since \(n>0\), we have \(d>0\). Also
\[
r=D(d)\le d=D(n)\le n. \tag{6}
\]
By applying (2) first to \(n\), and then to \(d\), we obtain
\[
n\equiv d\equiv r\pmod9.
\]
Together with \(r\le n\), this shows that \(n-r\) is a nonnegative multiple of \(9\). Thus \(t\) is a nonnegative integer and
\[
n=9t+r. \tag{7}
\]

In fact,
\[
t\ge2. \tag{8}
\]
If instead \(t\le1\), then, using (7), (6), and (1),
\[
n=9t+r\le9+d\le \left\lfloor\frac n{10}\right\rfloor+18.
\]
For \(n\ge21\), however,
\[
\left\lfloor\frac n{10}\right\rfloor+18
\le \frac n{10}+18<n,
\]
because \(n>20\). This is a contradiction.

We next show
\[
d\le t+10. \tag{9}
\]
From (1), interpreted as an ordinary rational inequality, and from (7),
\[
10d\le n+90=9t+r+90.
\]
Since \(r\le d\), this implies
\[
10d\le9t+d+90,
\]
and hence \(9d\le9t+90\), which is (9).

For every integer \(t\ge2\),
\[
t+10\le10^t. \tag{10}
\]
At \(t=2\), this is \(12\le100\). If it holds for some \(t\ge2\), then
\[
(t+1)+10=t+11\le10(t+10)\le10\cdot10^t=10^{t+1},
\]
so induction proves (10). Combining (9) and (10), we have
\[
d\le10^t. \tag{11}
\]

Define
\[
B=d(10^t-1).
\]
By (5) and (11),
\[
D(B)=9t. \tag{12}
\]
Let \(L\) be the number of decimal digits of \(B\). Notice that \(B>0\), because \(d>0\) and \(t\ge2\), and therefore \(B<10^L\). Now define
\[
K=B+10^L d.
\]
In decimal notation, this places the digits of \(d\) immediately to the left of the \(L\)-digit block representing \(B\). By block additivity (3), (12), and the definition of \(r\),
\[
D(K)=D(B)+D(d)=9t+r=n, \tag{13}
\]
where the last equality is (7). Moreover, \(d\) divides both terms in the definition of \(K\): it divides \(B=d(10^t-1)\), and it divides \(10^Ld\). Hence
\[
D(n)=d\mid K. \tag{14}
\]
Also \(K>0\).

If \(K\ne n\), equations (13) and (14) show directly that \(K\) is a partner of \(n\): indeed,
\[
D(n)\mid K
\quad\text{and}\quad
D(K)=n\mid n.
\]

There remains the possibility that the constructed \(K\) equals \(n\). In that case use
\[
K'=10K.
\]
Appending a zero does not change the digit sum, so
\[
D(K')=D(K)=n.
\]
Since \(d\mid K\), we also have \(d\mid10K=K'\). Thus
\[
D(n)\mid K'
\quad\text{and}\quad
D(K')=n\mid n.
\]
Finally, \(K'>0\), and because \(K=n>0\), we have \(K'=10K\ne K=n\). Hence \(K'\) is a partner of \(n\). This completes the construction for every \(n\ge21\).

It remains to handle \(1\le n\le20\). The following table gives an explicit partner \(k\) for each such \(n\), together with the relevant digit sums:
\[
\begin{array}{c|c|c|c}
n&k&D(n)&D(k)\\ \hline
1&10&1&1\\
2&20&2&2\\
3&30&3&3\\
4&40&4&4\\
5&50&5&5\\
6&60&6&6\\
7&70&7&7\\
8&80&8&8\\
9&90&9&9\\
10&1&1&1\\
11&10&2&1\\
12&3&3&3\\
13&100&4&1\\
14&10&5&1\\
15&12&6&3\\
16&35&7&8\\
17&1000&8&1\\
18&9&9&9\\
19&10&10&1\\
20&2&2&2
\end{array}
\]
Every listed \(k\) is positive and differs from \(n\). Directly from the table, \(D(n)\mid k\) and \(D(k)\mid n\) in every row. For example, the only slightly less immediate rows include \(n=13\), where \(4\mid100\) and \(1\mid13\); \(n=16\), where \(7\mid35\) and \(8\mid16\); and \(n=19\), where \(10\mid10\) and \(1\mid19\). Thus every positive \(n<21\) also has a partner.

We have therefore shown that for every positive integer \(n\), the set
\[
P_n=\{k\in\mathbb N:k>0,\ k\ne n,\ D(n)\mid k,\ D(k)\mid n\}
\]
is nonempty. By the well-ordering principle it has a least element, and by its defining condition that least element is positive. The sequence definition assigns this least element to \(a(n)\) whenever \(P_n\) is nonempty, assigning \(0\) only when \(P_n\) is empty. Since the latter case never occurs for positive \(n\), we conclude
\[
\boxed{a(n)\ne0\quad\text{for every positive integer }n.}
\]
